newsitem.title: HUNGARY: NOVARTIS HUNGARY UNIT SEES FLAT 1997 SALES.
newsitem.headline: NOVARTIS HUNGARY UNIT SEES FLAT 1997 SALES.

text.p: The Swiss pharmaceutical company Novartis's local unit expects flat sales in 1997 in Hungary, Novartis's biggest Central-East European market, the president of the Hungarian operations said.
"We essentially only expect sales to grow as much as inflation or possibly a little slower," Gary Phillips said.

Novartis was created last year by the merger of two Swiss drug firms, Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz. The Hungarian subsidiaries are currently in the process of merging and are expected to run under the name Novartis Magyarorszag Kft except for their seed units, which will be incorporated as Novartis Seed Kft.
The two subsidiaries's combined sales were 15.8 billion forints in 1996, of which drugs made up 8.5 billion, with the rest coming from the sale of agricultural chemicals and seeds, Phillips said.
The 1997 plans call for 10.3 billion forints of drug sales and 8.4 billion forints from agrobusiness in current (not inflation-adjusted) prices, he added.
Government estimates call for an about 17 percent increase in Hungarian consumer prices in 1997.
Stagnant drug sales will be the result of increased volumes and lower prices in real terms, said Andras Hajdu, the financial director-to-be of Novartis Magyarorszag.

"For the (subsidised) prescription drugs, the government strictly controls prices and we have agreed to a nine to 10 percent average increase only for 1997," he said. "But we expect an increase in our sales volume because we will be introducing new products and because of the launch of over-the-counter drugs."
He added that regulations concerning the sale of over-the-counter products, which barely exist in Hungary now, are currently being drafted.

In agricultural products the market is already saturated and Novartis, which is already the market leader in Hungary, expects to have to fight hard to maintain its 15 percent market share, Hajdu said.

In other countries in the region, Hajdu said that Novartis faced mixed prospects. The Czech division is far from reaching the Hungarian unit's sales, while in Poland the company was hampered by strict limits on drug imports.
